title: “Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle…
content: “Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. What four? Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble virtue, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble concentration … noble wisdom … noble liberation, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death.”

title: The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness, But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure. Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield…
content:
The foolish, ignorant person delights in heedlessness,
But the wise one guards heedlessness as his greatest treasure.
Do not yield to heedlessness, do not yield to sensual pleasures.

title: “Form, sound, taste, smell, touch — All these things Are desirable, delightful, agreeable As long as they exist. The world with its devas Regards them…
content:
“Form, sound, taste, smell, touch —
All these things
Are desirable, delightful, agreeable
As long as they exist.

The world with its devas
Regards them as delightful,
But when they cease,
Then they are seen as suffering.

The noble ones see as happiness
The destruction of identity.
This is completely opposite
To what the whole world sees.

What others call happiness,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as happiness.

The good have open eyes, they see, they have light —
Apart from the noble ones,
Who is worthy of perfect enlightenment?
By that right knowledge of the path,
They attain Nibbāna, free from defilements.”

title: Elder Talapuṭa: O mind, everywhere, I have acted as you wished, For many lives — You were not angry with me, And this inner-born body…
content:
Elder Talapuṭa:

O mind, everywhere,
I have acted as you wished,
For many lives —
You were not angry with me,
And this inner-born body
Is your gratitude!
On the long path of saṃsāra,
Suffering was caused by you.

O mind, you yourself made
This person that I am —
You made me become
A brahmin,
A king, a royal,
One day a merchant,
Another day a servant,
Or a kind of deity —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

Due to your power,
We became asuras —
Due to you,
I fell to the bottom of hell;
Sometimes an animal,
Sometimes a hungry ghost —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

You will not deceive me
Again, many times more,
Like sorcerers
Performing magic tricks.
You played tricks on me,
Like playing with a madman.
O mind, tell me —
Where have I wronged you?

Formerly this mind wandered,
Went wherever it wished,
Went where it delighted,
Went where it enjoyed —
Now I will restrain it
With wise reflection,
As with a hook one restrains
A rutting elephant.

For me, the Teacher
Has declared that life is impermanent —
Life is not eternal,
Life has no core.
O mind, urge me
To leap into the Buddha’s teaching —
Make me cross the flood,
So very hard to cross.

I have now gone forth
In the Great Sage’s Dhamma —
Those like me
Do not accept loss.

Forests, oceans, rivers, land,
The four directions, above and below —
All are impermanent.
The three realms are perilous.
O mind, where will you go?
You will enjoy peace.

title: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
content: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises. Sounds … Odors … Tastes … Touches … Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises.”

title: “Furthermore, Meghiya, for a monk well established in these five things, four more things are to be developed: foulness should be developed to abandon greed;…
content: “Furthermore, Meghiya, for a monk well established in these five things, four more things are to be developed: foulness should be developed to abandon greed; loving-kindness should be developed to abandon ill-will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed to cut off thoughts; the perception of impermanence should be developed to uproot the conceit ‘I am.’ For one with the perception of impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of not-self becomes established. For one with the perception of not-self, the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am’ is attained, Nibbāna in this very life.”

title: “Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, one, two, or…
content:
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, one, two, or three days dead – bloated, discolored, festering. What do you think, monks? Has the former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?”
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms.”

title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen wholesome states arise and arisen unwholesome states decline, as fewness of wishes. For one…
content: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen wholesome states arise and arisen unwholesome states decline, as fewness of wishes. For one with few wishes, monks, unarisen wholesome states arise and arisen unwholesome states decline.”

title: “And, monks, when that monk dwells in these five things, four more things should be developed. The perception of foulness should be developed to abandon…
content: “And, monks, when that monk dwells in these five things, four more things should be developed. The perception of foulness should be developed to abandon greed; loving-kindness should be developed to abandon ill-will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed to cut off thoughts; the perception of impermanence should be developed to uproot the conceit ‘I am.’ For a monk with the perception of impermanence, monks, the perception of not-self becomes established. For one with the perception of not-self, the conceit ‘I am’ is uprooted, and Nibbāna is attained in this very life.”

title: Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One: How can one cross the flood, Steadfast and persevering day and…
content:
Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One:
How can one cross the flood,
Steadfast and persevering day and night?
Without stalling, without clinging —
Who does not sink in the abyss?

(The Blessed One):
One who always has virtue,
Wisdom, and is well-concentrated,
With aroused energy and strength —
That one crosses the hard-to-cross flood.
One who has abandoned perception of lust,
Who has crossed beyond the fetter of form,
Who has destroyed delight and craving for existence —
That one does not sink in the abyss.
